entities.summary:
Ancient China refers to Chinese civilization from its earliest known organized states (Xia dynasty, c. 2070 BCE, if historical) through the Shang (c. 1600-1046 BCE) and Zhou (1046-256 BCE) dynasties — the formative period when Chinese writing, bronze metallurgy, silk production, ancestor worship, the Mandate of Heaven political theology, Confucianism, Daoism, and Legalism were established, creating the cultural, philosophical, and political foundations that shaped Chinese civilization for 4,000 years. The Zhou's Spring and Autumn period (771-476 BCE) was China's 'Axial Age' — producing Confucius, Laozi, and Sunzi simultaneously.

The Shang dynasty (c. 1600-1046 BCE) produced oracle bone script (the earliest confirmed Chinese writing), massive bronze ritual vessels (the Simuwu Ding is a Shang creation), horse-drawn chariots, and systematic ancestor worship. Shang kings communicated with ancestors through oracle bones — tortoise shells or ox scapulae heated until cracked, with cracks interpreted as divine answers. The Zhou overthrew the Shang (1046 BCE) using the 'Mandate of Heaven' (tianming) theology: rulers lose heaven's mandate through immoral governance, justifying revolution.

The Zhou Spring and Autumn Period (771-476 BCE) saw the 'Hundred Schools of Thought' — Confucius (551-479 BCE) teaching moral self-cultivation and ethical governance; Laozi (6th century BCE, if historical) teaching the Dao; Sunzi (544-496 BCE) writing The Art of War. These texts — the Analects, the Tao Te Ching, and The Art of War — are among the most influential books in world history. The Warring States Period (475-221 BCE) ended with Qin unification creating Imperial China.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ancient China — establishing Chinese writing, Mandate of Heaven, Confucianism, Daoism, and Legalism simultaneously during the Zhou Axial Age — created the philosophical and political foundations that governed the world's most populous civilization for 4,000 years, making it one of the most consequential cultural formations in human history.
